ios.image: `leaving drops every frame and node` reads the engine's frame and node counters (`SvelteEngine.foreignStats`), which exist on Android only: one check fewer in each place.
ios.blur: `leaving drops every frame and node` reads the engine's frame and node counters (`SvelteEngine.foreignStats`), which exist on Android only: one check fewer in each place.
ios.gradient: `leaving drops every frame and node` reads the engine's frame and node counters (`SvelteEngine.foreignStats`), which exist on Android only: one check fewer in each place.
ios.video: Five checks fewer in each place, all of them Android facts: the frame and node counters (`SvelteEngine.foreignStats`), the player's own `SurfaceView` or `TextureView` (an `AVPlayerLayer` is a layer of the view and has no surface to list), the capture without `handleGLSurfaceViewOnAndroid` being a hole, the capture with it holding the frame (a snapshot of the view hierarchy does not hold an `AVPlayerLayer`'s video frames: transparent on the iPhone, 4 Nov 2026), and `two volume changes raise both onVolumeChange although the JS thread was busy`, which guards a defect of the Android event class (`VideoCustomEvent` coalesced in React Native's event queue; `patches/react-native-video@6.19.3.patch`). iOS's RCTVideo is a legacy view manager whose events React Native's interop layer sends with `dispatchEvent`, which the queue never replaces.
ios.datetime: Android's picker is a dialog window the module opens, dismisses and answers (`openDatePicker`, `dismissDatePicker`, the buttons the harness presses with `adb`), and the frame and node counters are Android's: those checks are Android-only on the iPhone. iOS's picker is a view (`RNDateTimePickerComponentView` holding a `UIDatePicker`) with six checks of its own in each place (the value prop, the date the handler stores, a new value, the mode, `onValueChange`, `onDismiss`), so the iPhone makes more checks than Android's bar of nine per place, which counts the dialog checks that need no press.
ios.lottie: Two checks fewer in each place, both Android's: `leaving drops every frame and node` reads the engine's frame and node counters (`SvelteEngine.foreignStats`), and `two cancelled animations raise both onAnimationFinish although the JS thread was busy` guards a defect of the Android event classes (coalesced in React Native's event queue; `patches/lottie-react-native@7.3.8.patch`). iOS sends the events through the codegen emitter's `dispatchEvent`, which the queue never replaces.
ios.pdf: Two checks fewer in each place, both Android's: `leaving drops every frame and node` reads the engine's frame and node counters (`SvelteEngine.foreignStats`), and `onLoadComplete arrives although the JS thread was busy while the document loaded` guards a defect of the Android view (its one `topChange` event coalesced in React Native's event queue; `patches/react-native-pdf@7.0.3.patch`). iOS sends `onChange` through the codegen emitter's `dispatchEvent`, which the queue never replaces, and loads the document again only when `path` changes, not for the page prop that reloads it on Android.
ios.capture: `leaving drops every frame and node` reads the engine's frame and node counters (`SvelteEngine.foreignStats`), which exist on Android only: one check fewer in each place.
ios.rive: Two checks fewer in each place, both Android's: `leaving drops every frame and node` reads the engine's frame and node counters (`SvelteEngine.foreignStats`), and `two animations played in turn raise both onPlay although the JS thread was busy`, which guards that Rive's Android events keep reaching JavaScript one by one. Nothing is patched for it: Rive sends them through React Native's interop emitter (`getJSModule(RCTEventEmitter)`), which is made with the application context, so its events have surface id -1 and are sent as non-coalescable. There is nothing to lose on iOS: `RiveReactNativeView` is a legacy view manager whose events React Native's interop layer sends with `dispatchEvent`, which the queue never replaces.
ios.conic: `leaving drops every frame and node` reads the engine's frame and node counters (`SvelteEngine.foreignStats`), which exist on Android only: one check fewer in each place.
ios.shadow: react-native-fast-shadow has no iOS code (`ShadowedView` is React Native's `View` and the shadow is the layer's own), so the four checks of its Android view and of the engine's canvas clip, and the frame and node counters, are Android-only: five checks fewer in each place. The press on the shadowed child needs a finger, which the lab has none of on the iPhone (XCUITest does not run on it): it is skipped in each place, a sixth check fewer, so `skipped` is 3, not 0.
ios.text: `leaving drops every frame and node` reads the engine's frame and node counters (`SvelteEngine.foreignStats`), which exist on Android only: one check fewer in each place.
ios.svg: The frame and node counters (`SvelteEngine.foreignStats`) are Android's: one check fewer in each place. The press on the `Svg` needs a finger, which the lab has none of on the iPhone (XCUITest does not run on it): it is skipped in each place, a second check fewer, so `skipped` is 3, not 0.
